claims.text: Elevated-temperature stability of nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal HENA is not determined solely by configurational entropy.
Suppression of phase separation by sluggish diffusion kinetics is critical to HENA structural stability.
A spinodal-decomposition driving force that exceeds the sluggish-diffusion kinetic barrier will cause rapid nanoprecipitation and grain coarsening without external stress.
PtRuIrRhPd can form an equimolar five-component nanoparticle alloy produced by carbothermal shock.
Non-equilibrium synthesis of the proposed TiCoCrFeMn or PtRuIrRhPd nanoparticles produces a single-phase solid solution with high lattice distortion and no pre-existing precipitates.
The proposed nanoparticles should be annealed at 800–1000 °C for 10–1000 hours in an inert atmosphere while composition is varied toward a spinodal boundary.
The relevant sluggish-diffusion coefficients are orders of magnitude below those of conventional alloys and are approximately 10^-19 m^2 s^-1.
The cocktail effect associated with lattice distortion contributes a kinetic barrier against phase separation.
High configurational entropy thermodynamically stabilizes a single-phase solid solution.
Structural evolution is governed by competition between the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation and kinetic resistance from sluggish diffusion.
Negative mixing enthalpy of pairs such as Ni-Al or Ti-Cr drives phase separation.
A sufficiently large thermodynamic driving force will produce ordered B2 or Laves nanoprecipitates.
Long thermal exposure can cause grain growth and a reduction in hardness in TiCoCrFeMn.
High-driving-force compositions will show an initial reconstruction and chemical-fluctuation period followed by nanoprecipitate nucleation and accelerated grain growth after a critical time.
Nanoprecipitation and grain growth will cause loss of the single-phase structure and decreased hardness or stability.

Traditional binary or ternary alloys typically undergo immediate phase separation or rapid grain growth at elevated temperature because they have lower diffusion barriers and lack configurational-entropy stabilization.
Conventional HEAs with low thermodynamic driving forces maintain single-phase stability for long durations.
Low mixing free energy or compositions far from the spinodal region allow sluggish diffusion to suppress atomic rearrangement over the experimental timescale.
For particles larger than 100 nm, surface-energy effects dominate over bulk diffusion kinetics.

Persistence of a single phase with no nanoprecipitates and a grain-growth rate below 0.001 µm h^-1 after 1000 hours at 1000 °C in a high-driving-force composition would falsify the proposed intrinsic-instability mechanism.
